fr:title.text: Theories are schemas, models are instances

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Theories are schemas, models are instances

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In geolog, we use the word theory to mean a type used as a database schema, and we say model to refer to an element of a theory, which you might also think of as a database instance on the schema described by that theory.

We now show how to build up progressively more complex theories via different type formers. In order to give an intuition for what each of these type formers means, we also describe how to interact with models of those theories via the TypeScript FFI (note: the TypeScript FFI is a work in progress at the moment).
Set is a theory, and models of Set are collections of things. This corresponds to a very simple kind of database by itself, but we can do many things from this foundation.
We refer to models of Set as, unsurprisingly, “sets.”
In TypeScript, models of Set store collections of Values, where Value is defined in the following way
All elements in the collection should be of the same type (e.g. all row ids, all strings, etc.) but for simplicity all sets share the same untyped API involving Values.
A TypeScript value m that refers to a model of Set satisfies the following interface
If m has read-write permissions, then it will also satisfy the interface

Intuitively, add() does not take parameters because it adds a fresh element to the set, an element not equal to any other previous element. This means that a set of integers can never be read-write because it is impossible to create a fresh integer. We will see later on that it is instead possible to store a subset of the set of all integers; this will look differently however.
For a set with read-write permission, the following code should not throw an error.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: const a = m.add() assert(m.has(a))

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Records types are a way of composing multiple theories into one theory. A record type has multiple fields, each of which is declared to be a model of another theory. For instance:
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: theory SantaList := sig naughty : Set nice : Set end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: SantaList is a very simple theory, the models of which consist of a pair of a collection of naughty things and a collection of nice things.

More precisely, if we have a model m of SantaList in TypeScript, then m.naughty and m.nice are both models of Set. If m is readonly, then m.naughty and m.nice will satisfy ReadonlySet, and if m is read-write, then m.naughty and m.nice will satisfy ReadWriteSet. The following TypeScript code should run without errors if m is a read-write model of SantaList.
A model A : Set may itself be used as a theory. A model of A is just an element of A (remember that a model of Set is a collection of things). For example, consider the following theory.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: theory PopulatedSantaList := sig list : SantaList john : list.nice mary : list.naughty end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: A model m of PopulatedSantaList consists of a model m.list of SantaList, along with specific elements m.john in m.list.nice and m.mary in m.list.naughty.
In TypeScript, an element of a set comes along with a getter, and if it is read-write, also a setter. So if m is a TypeScript variable accessing a model of PopulatedSantaList, then we should have:
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: assert(m.list.nice.has(m.john.get()))
fr:mainmatter.html:p: If m is incomplete, then m.john.get() might return null. This would be the case in a freshly-created model, as in
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: const m = PopulatedSantaList.create()
fr:mainmatter.html:p: This can be remedied by using .set(), as in
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: const john = m.list.nice.add() m.john.set(john)
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Note that m.john.set(x) would throw an exception if x were not in m.list.nice.
Function types are theories, as long as the domain is a set and the codomain is a theory.
Function types can be used in many ways. Here are some examples.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: theory StateMachine := sig state : Set next : state -> state end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: If we have m : StateMachine, then m.next is a function that sends elements of m.state to other elements of m.state. fr:mainmatter.html:pre: const m = StateMachine.create() const [x,y] = [m.state.add(), m.state.add()] m.next(x).set(y) m.next(y).set(y)
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Note that at the point where we have added x and y but not yet set the values of next for them, m is not a valid instance for StateMachine. Another way of creating interesting propositions is with equality. Given two elements a0 and a1 of a set A, there is a proposition a0 = a1 which is true if and only if a0 is equal to a1.
We can use this to write down laws in our theories that involve equality. For instance, we can write down the theory of a two-way mapping (mathematically known as a bijection) in the following way
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: theory TwoWayMapping (X : Set) (Y : Set) := sig fwd : X -> Y bwd : Y -> X bwd-fwd : (x : X) -> bwd (fwd x) = x fwd-bwd : (y : Y) -> fwd (bwd x) = x end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Another example of equality usage is when we assert that a relation is a partial function, by saying that if x is related to both y0 and y1 then y0 must be equal to y1.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: theory IsPartialFunction (X : Set) (Y : Set) (R : X -> Y -> Prop) := (x : X) -> (y0 y1 : Y) -> R x y0 -> R x y1 -> y0 = y1
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Equality is useful for constraints, but is especially useful for queries.

These six type formers (The theory of sets, Record types as theories, Sets as theories, Function types as theories, Propositions and relations and Equality types as theories) can be used to compositionally build up fairly complex combinatorial structures of sets, functions and relations. However, they are still limited when it comes to handling data, which often has, for instance, numbers and strings in it.

We could simply put in String and Int in as “base sets”. However, this would permit functions String -> String, and we cannot store a function like that in a database because the set of strings is infinite and the function must be total, so storing the value of the function at every string would take infinite storage. We could say that String was a theory and not a set, which would prevent it from being used in the domain of a function, but it is perfectly sensible to have the theory String -> Prop (which denotes a subset of the set of all strings), and making String a theory would prevent us from forming that.

The solution to this problem requires building up a little more theory, so we do not address it right now, and instead continue on to give a full account of the “purely combinatorial” fragment of geolog.

fr:title.text: Sets are queries, elements are results

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Sets are queries, elements are results

fr:mainmatter.html:p: One can query a database in geolog via for-loops in TypeScript, but this is obviously not the most efficient or ergonomic way to do it. In fact, we already have the machinery to write down queries, it just requires a bit of rethinking what we have already learned. The idea is that giving a way to produce a set from a model of a theory is a query. The elements of that set are the results of the query.

Just like we have record types as the theory-level, we also have record types at the set-level. We can use this to define a set in the context of a model of a given theory; this is how to “natively query” an instance of a geolog theory.todo
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: def jealousy-triangle (m : Drama) : Set := tuple a : m.person b : m.person c : m.person a-b : m.jealous-of a b b-c : m.jealous-of b c c-a : m.jealous-of c a end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: In TypeScript, jealousy-triangle is compiled to a function that takes in a model of Drama and returns a ReadonlySet.todo The elements v of this ReadonlySet are Values with the "tuple" tag, which have fields a,b,c that are elements of m.person, such that m.jealous-of(v.value.a)(v.value.b).isTrue(), and so on. The value v will also have v.value.a_b, but it will just be null, thought of as the unique element of the singleton set.

Iterating through the elements of jealousy_triangle(m) will be faster than the naive approach of a triply-nested for-loop over m.person and then filtering out using m.jealous-of, because geolog can plan the query and take advantage of fast join algorithms on the m.jealous-of table.todo
This query can be written more compactly in the following way.todo
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: def jealousy-triangle (m : Drama) : Set := tuple a b c : m.person m.jealous-of a b m.jealous-of b c m.jealous-of c a end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: We can omit the field names for propositions because we never need to refer to the witnesses of the propositions, we just need the propositions to be true.
As a variation on the same theme, we could look for length-3 cycles in a state machine with
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: def next-triangle (m : StateMachine) : Set := tuple a b c : m.state m.next a = b m.next b = c m.next c = a end

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In the queries, we saw several usages of the pattern
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: def query (m : T) : Set := ...
fr:mainmatter.html:p: def is in fact a much more general construct; any theory can replace Set on the right, and we can take in multiple arguments.
In general, this allows one to create a view of a model one theory, in the form of a model of another theory.

fr:title.text: Elements of record types as views

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Elements of record types as views

fr:mainmatter.html:p: If a theory is given by a record type (using sig ... end), then we can produce a model of it using struct ... end, setting all of its fields. For example, we can reward the wrong children with the following code (using SantaList from Record types as theories).
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: def santa-mixup (m : SantaList) : SantaList := struct naughty := m.nice nice := m.naughty end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: When using struct, one must give all the fields of the original record type in the same order as they were originally defined.
With some slightly more complex code, we can produce a model of SantaList from a model of SantaLists and a choice of year.

Intuitively, this assigns naughty to the set of children naughty in that year, and similarly with nice. The tuple syntax is just as in Record types as sets, using the curly-brace inline syntax. And m.list y .naughty child is just a sequence of function applications and field projection. Walking through the types, we have m.list : m.person -> SantaListOver m.person, so m .list y : SantaListOver m.person and then m.list y .naughty : m.person -> Prop and finally m.list y .naughty child : Prop.

fr:title.text: Elements of function types as views

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Elements of function types as views

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Just as we can produce elements of record types with struct ... end, we can produce elements of function types with lambda syntax x => a, just like anonymous functions in Javascript.
As an example, we can produce the graph of a function, which is a binary relation on the domain and codomain.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: def graph (X : Set) (Y : Set) (f : X -> Y) : X -> Y -> Prop := x => y => f x = y
fr:mainmatter.html:p: We can also now start making some non-trivial views of theories that involve function types. For instance, we could run a state-machine at double speed.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: def double-time (m : StateMachine) : StateMachine := struct state := m.state next := x => m.next (m.next x) end

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In Basic types we learned:

html:ul.html:li: How to use theory and def. These are the only two top-level declarations in geolog, so we have now learned all of the top-level declarations.
How to use Set, Prop, sets, record types, function types and equality types to build up theories.
How to produce some models of theories from other models.

Instead, we can just run m.jealous_of(john)(sue).makeTrue(), and the model will be valid again. This is because if the codomain of a function is a proposition, there is ultimately only one possible way for that function to exist, and thus the function need not be explicitly defined. We discuss how this works in a later section.todo
Another way of creating interesting propositions is with equality. Given two elements a0 and a1 of a set A, there is a proposition a0 = a1 which is true if and only if a0 is equal to a1.
We can use this to write down laws in our theories that involve equality. For instance, we can write down the theory of a two-way mapping (mathematically known as a bijection) in the following way
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: theory TwoWayMapping (X : Set) (Y : Set) := sig fwd : X -> Y bwd : Y -> X bwd-fwd : (x : X) -> bwd (fwd x) = x fwd-bwd : (y : Y) -> fwd (bwd x) = x end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Another example of equality usage is when we assert that a relation is a partial function, by saying that if x is related to both y0 and y1 then y0 must be equal to y1.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: theory IsPartialFunction (X : Set) (Y : Set) (R : X -> Y -> Prop) := (x : X) -> (y0 y1 : Y) -> R x y0 -> R x y1 -> y0 = y1
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Equality is useful for constraints, but is especially useful for queries.

These six type formers (The theory of sets, Record types as theories, Sets as theories, Function types as theories, Propositions and relations and Equality types as theories) can be used to compositionally build up fairly complex combinatorial structures of sets, functions and relations. However, they are still limited when it comes to handling data, which often has, for instance, numbers and strings in it.

We could simply put in String and Int in as “base sets”. However, this would permit functions String -> String, and we cannot store a function like that in a database because the set of strings is infinite and the function must be total, so storing the value of the function at every string would take infinite storage. We could say that String was a theory and not a set, which would prevent it from being used in the domain of a function, but it is perfectly sensible to have the theory String -> Prop (which denotes a subset of the set of all strings), and making String a theory would prevent us from forming that.

The solution to this problem requires building up a little more theory, so we do not address it right now, and instead continue on to give a full account of the “purely combinatorial” fragment of geolog.

fr:title.text: Sets are queries, elements are results

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Sets are queries, elements are results

fr:mainmatter.html:p: One can query a database in geolog via for-loops in TypeScript, but this is obviously not the most efficient or ergonomic way to do it. In fact, we already have the machinery to write down queries, it just requires a bit of rethinking what we have already learned. The idea is that giving a way to produce a set from a model of a theory is a query. The elements of that set are the results of the query.

Just like we have record types as the theory-level, we also have record types at the set-level. We can use this to define a set in the context of a model of a given theory; this is how to “natively query” an instance of a geolog theory.todo
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: def jealousy-triangle (m : Drama) : Set := tuple a : m.person b : m.person c : m.person a-b : m.jealous-of a b b-c : m.jealous-of b c c-a : m.jealous-of c a end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: In TypeScript, jealousy-triangle is compiled to a function that takes in a model of Drama and returns a ReadonlySet.todo The elements v of this ReadonlySet are Values with the "tuple" tag, which have fields a,b,c that are elements of m.person, such that m.jealous-of(v.value.a)(v.value.b).isTrue(), and so on. The value v will also have v.value.a_b, but it will just be null, thought of as the unique element of the singleton set.

Iterating through the elements of jealousy_triangle(m) will be faster than the naive approach of a triply-nested for-loop over m.person and then filtering out using m.jealous-of, because geolog can plan the query and take advantage of fast join algorithms on the m.jealous-of table.todo
This query can be written more compactly in the following way.todo
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: def jealousy-triangle (m : Drama) : Set := tuple a b c : m.person m.jealous-of a b m.jealous-of b c m.jealous-of c a end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: We can omit the field names for propositions because we never need to refer to the witnesses of the propositions, we just need the propositions to be true.
As a variation on the same theme, we could look for length-3 cycles in a state machine with
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: def next-triangle (m : StateMachine) : Set := tuple a b c : m.state m.next a = b m.next b = c m.next c = a end

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In the queries, we saw several usages of the pattern
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: def query (m : T) : Set := ...
fr:mainmatter.html:p: def is in fact a much more general construct; any theory can replace Set on the right, and we can take in multiple arguments.
In general, this allows one to create a view of a model one theory, in the form of a model of another theory.

fr:title.text: Elements of record types as views

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Elements of record types as views

fr:mainmatter.html:p: If a theory is given by a record type (using sig ... end), then we can produce a model of it using struct ... end, setting all of its fields. For example, we can reward the wrong children with the following code (using SantaList from Record types as theories).
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: def santa-mixup (m : SantaList) : SantaList := struct naughty := m.nice nice := m.naughty end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: When using struct, one must give all the fields of the original record type in the same order as they were originally defined.
With some slightly more complex code, we can produce a model of SantaList from a model of SantaLists and a choice of year.

Intuitively, this assigns naughty to the set of children naughty in that year, and similarly with nice. The tuple syntax is just as in Record types as sets, using the curly-brace inline syntax. And m.list y .naughty child is just a sequence of function applications and field projection. Walking through the types, we have m.list : m.person -> SantaListOver m.person, so m .list y : SantaListOver m.person and then m.list y .naughty : m.person -> Prop and finally m.list y .naughty child : Prop.

fr:title.text: Elements of function types as views

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Elements of function types as views

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Just as we can produce elements of record types with struct ... end, we can produce elements of function types with lambda syntax x => a, just like anonymous functions in Javascript.
As an example, we can produce the graph of a function, which is a binary relation on the domain and codomain.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: def graph (X : Set) (Y : Set) (f : X -> Y) : X -> Y -> Prop := x => y => f x = y
fr:mainmatter.html:p: We can also now start making some non-trivial views of theories that involve function types. For instance, we could run a state-machine at double speed.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: def double-time (m : StateMachine) : StateMachine := struct state := m.state next := x => m.next (m.next x) end

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In Basic types we learned:

html:ul.html:li: How to use theory and def. These are the only two top-level declarations in geolog, so we have now learned all of the top-level declarations.
How to use Set, Prop, sets, record types, function types and equality types to build up theories.
How to produce some models of theories from other models.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In Inductive types, we will see how to produce more models of theories, which will in turn allow us to produce more theories. However, the basic structure introduced here will remain more or less the same.
Function types are theories, as long as the domain is a set and the codomain is a theory.
Function types can be used in many ways. Here are some examples.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: theory StateMachine := sig state : Set next : state -> state end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: If we have m : StateMachine, then m.next is a function that sends elements of m.state to other elements of m.state. The type state -> state satisfies the criterion for being a theory because its domain is a set and its codomain is a theory (following Sets as theories). Concretely, in TypeScript, we could use this like
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: const m = StateMachine.create() const [x,y] = [m.state.add(), m.state.add()] m.next(x).set(y) m.next(y).set(y)
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Note that at the point where we have added x and y but not yet set the values of next for them, m is not a valid instance for StateMachine. In fact, in general it is inevitable that in the process of building a model one may pass through an invalid state. Thus, validity is only checked at certain points; we discuss validity more in a later section.todo
But that is not all functions can do. As the codomain of a function can be a theory, we could also do the following.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: theory SantaLists := sig year : Set list : year -> SantaList end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: From TypeScript, we could use a model m of SantaLists in the following way.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: const y2025 = m.year.add() const bob = m.list(y2025).nice.add()
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Now, there are some ontological problems with this database schema. We cannot ask whether a person is nice one year and naughty the other year, because the nice and naughty sets for each year are disjoint. What we would really like is there to be one set of people, and then in different years they might be nice or naughty. This can be accomplished with relations.
